meta.question: How do production agents detect that they are stuck in a loop, and what do they do about it?
meta.title: Loop detection
meta.hook: Gemini CLI asks a model if the agent is looping. OpenHands matches patterns. LangGraph just counts steps.

answer: There is no single technique. Gemini CLI runs three detectors: hashed tool-call cycles [^g-cycle], repeated text [^g-contentdoc], and a periodic model-based check [^g-llmgate] that a second model is asked to confirm [^g-double]. OpenHands matches rule-based patterns over the recent event history [^o-scenarios]. Gemini CLI warns the model on a first detection [^g-turnstart][^g-recover], and OpenHands does so for repeated errors [^o-nudge]. LangGraph has no behavioural detection, only a step budget [^l-tick], and no loop detector was found in Codex.

repos.summary: A dedicated `LoopDetectionService` with three detectors [^g-cycle][^g-contentdoc][^g-llmgate], a one-time recovery message [^g-recover], and a hard stop on the second detection [^g-turnstart].

repos.what: The agent SDK and server behind OpenHands (the OpenHands/OpenHands repository is now the UI)
repos.summary: A `StuckDetector` that tests recent actions and observations against a set of stuck patterns [^o-scenarios], four of which are implemented [^o-stub]. It nudges the model on a repeated error [^o-nudge] and otherwise marks the conversation `STUCK` [^o-run].
The runtime does not look at behaviour. It counts steps [^l-tick] and raises `GraphRecursionError` at the limit [^l-raise]; recognising an unproductive loop is left to the graph you write.

No loop detector or step cap was found in the core turn loop at this commit. Follow-up is needed when the model asks for it or input is pending [^x-followup]; when it is needed the loop goes round again [^x-continue], and there is a branch for when it is not [^x-exit].

deep_dives.headline: Three detectors, one warning, then a stop
how_it_works: Every stream event passes through `addAndCheck` [^g-events]. For tool calls the service hashes the tool name plus its JSON arguments with SHA-256 [^g-key] and looks for a repeating cycle: any pattern of length 1 to 5 that has repeated 5 times in a row [^g-cycle][^g-toolthr]. That catches `A A A A A` and also `A B A B A B A B A B`.

For model text, it works in 50-character chunks [^g-contentconst], hashes them, and flags a loop when identical chunks appear frequently within a short distance; detection is switched off inside code blocks [^g-contentdoc]. A chunk has to occur at least 10 times before its spacing is tested [^g-contentthr].

Neither catches an agent that keeps doing slightly different unproductive things. So once a single prompt has run for 30 turns [^g-llmconst][^g-llmgate], the service periodically sends recent history to a model [^g-history]. If that model's confidence is below 0.9, nothing is reported [^g-below][^g-conf]. At 0.9 or above, a second model alias is asked to double-check [^g-double], and a loop is reported if it also reaches the threshold [^g-confirm]. If the second model is unavailable, the first model's verdict is used alone [^g-unavailable]. The interval between checks adapts between 5 and 15 turns [^g-interval]: the higher the last confidence, the sooner the next check [^g-adapt].

The response is graduated. On the first detection `GeminiClient` clears the flag, injects a message telling the model a potential loop was detected, and continues [^g-recover], unless the turn budget is already used up, in which case it stops with `MaxSessionTurns` [^g-turnstart]. On the second detection it emits `LoopDetected` and ends the turn [^g-turnstart].

gotchas: The tool-call key is an exact hash of name and arguments [^g-key], so a call with one changed argument counts as a different call.
The model-based check costs extra model calls, and only starts after 30 turns in one prompt [^g-llmconst].
The double-check is skipped when the second model is unavailable: the first model's result is then enough to declare a loop [^g-unavailable].
Loop detection can be disabled by configuration or for the rest of a session [^g-disable].

deep_dives.headline: Four working patterns over a window of recent events
how_it_works: `StuckDetector.is_stuck` looks only at events after the last user message, within a window of recent events [^o-window], so a new instruction resets the picture. It runs its checks in a fixed order [^o-scenarios].

Four checks are implemented: the same action producing the same observation [^o-s1]; the same action followed by an error more times than the threshold [^o-s2]; consecutive agent messages with no action [^o-mono]; and an alternating action-observation pattern [^o-alt]. A fifth, for context-window errors, is a stub that always returns False [^o-stub]. The default thresholds are 4, 3, 3 and 6 [^o-thr].

The error check counts how many times in a row the latest action has been followed by an error event; it does not compare the errors with each other [^o-streak]. When that streak is exactly 3, `get_action_error_nudge` returns a message naming the tool and the latest error, and it fires only once per error event [^o-nudge]. The conversation injects it as a user-role message [^o-run]. If the streak goes past the threshold, the conversation is stuck [^o-s2].

When a pattern matches, the run loop's check sets the execution status to `STUCK` and returns True [^o-run]. Detection can be switched off [^o-defaults] and the thresholds overridden [^o-thrparam] when creating the conversation.

The context-window error check is not implemented at this commit: it returns False [^o-stub].

deep_dives.headline: A step counter, and the rest is up to you
how_it_works: LangGraph runs a graph in steps. When a run starts, the loop computes a stop point: the current step plus `recursion_limit` plus 1 [^l-stop]. On each tick it checks whether the step has passed that point and, if so, sets its status to `out_of_steps` [^l-tick].

The caller then raises `GraphRecursionError`, with a message suggesting a higher limit [^l-raise]. The default limit [^l-defaultuse] is read from an environment variable and is 10007 at this commit [^l-default].

The prebuilt ReAct agent adds one courtesy on top. If the model asks for more tool calls with fewer than 2 steps remaining [^l-more], it replaces the response with a short message saying it needs more steps [^l-sorry]. That message has no tool calls, so the agent's routing does not go back to the tools [^l-end].

Nothing in these paths inspects what the agent is doing: the only test is the step count [^l-tick]. If you want to notice the same tool being called repeatedly, you add that as a node or a check in your own graph.

deep_dives.headline: No detector found: the loop trusts the model and compaction
how_it_works: Codex's core turn function runs a loop. Its documentation says the model replies with function calls or an assistant message, and a function call's output is sent back in the next sampling request [^x-doc]. Follow-up is needed when the model asks for it or input is pending [^x-followup], and in that case the loop continues to its next iteration [^x-continue]. It has a branch for when none is needed [^x-exit], and breaks when the stop outcome says to stop [^x-break].

No code was found in `codex-rs/core` that compares successive tool calls, counts repeats or caps the number of passes. The one place the code mentions an infinite loop is a comment about compaction keeping the context below the token limit [^x-comment].
So at this layer nothing was found that judges whether the agent is making progress.

differences.title: Exact match versus judgment
differences.detail: Gemini CLI and OpenHands both start with exact matching [^g-key][^o-s1], which is cheap. Only Gemini CLI adds a model as judge for loops that exact matching cannot see [^g-llmgate], and it pays for that with extra model calls.

differences.title: Call only, or call plus result
differences.detail: Gemini CLI hashes the tool call alone [^g-key]. OpenHands requires the observations to match too [^o-s1], so polling a command whose output changes is not treated as a loop.

differences.title: Both can warn before they stop
differences.detail: Gemini CLI injects a warning on the first detection [^g-recover] and stops on the second [^g-turnstart]. OpenHands nudges only for a repeated error [^o-nudge]; a matched pattern sets the stuck status [^o-run].

differences.title: Products detect, the framework budgets
differences.detail: The two products that implement detection own the whole loop, so they can watch it. LangGraph does not know what your nodes mean, so it offers a step budget and leaves behaviour to you.

differences.title: How long before a hard cap
differences.detail: The step caps differ by two orders of magnitude: 100 turns per send in Gemini CLI [^g-maxturns][^g-cap], 500 iterations per run in OpenHands [^o-defaults], 10007 steps by default in LangGraph [^l-default][^l-defaultuse].

build_your_own: Start with a step cap. It is one line, and it is the only protection LangGraph gives you by default.
Add exact-match detection on tool calls: hash the name and arguments, keep a short history, and look for cycles, not only identical consecutive calls. Gemini CLI's version is under 40 lines.
Compare results as well as calls if your agent legitimately polls. OpenHands' action-plus-observation rule avoids that false positive.
Warn the model before stopping it. Gemini CLI does this on a first detection and OpenHands on repeated errors, and a message naming the tool and the error gives the model something to act on.
Give 'stuck' its own status, separate from error and finished, so callers and UIs can respond differently.
Only add a model-based check if exact matching is missing real loops, and gate it the way Gemini CLI does: after many turns, at a high confidence threshold, confirmed by a second model.

method.scope: Each repository was fetched at the commit listed above. For Gemini CLI, OpenHands and LangGraph the detection code and its call sites were read. For Codex the core turn loop's exit conditions were read and the core crate was searched for the terms listed in its section.
limits: OpenHands refers to the `OpenHands/software-agent-sdk` repository, where the agent logic lives; the `OpenHands/OpenHands` repository is now the user interface.
The Codex finding is 'not found in the core crate', not proof of absence across the whole product.
Gemini CLI's text-repetition detector and the internals of its model-based check were read but are not quoted in full.
Behaviour was read from source, not observed by running the agents.
OpenHands' context-window error check is a stub at this commit, so the report counts four working patterns.

g-key.claim: A tool call's key is the SHA-256 hash of its name joined with the JSON string of its arguments.

g-cycle.claim: For each cycle length from 1 to 5, a loop is reported when the last calls match that cycle repeated the threshold number of times.

g-contentconst.claim: The content loop threshold is 10 and the content chunk size is 50.

g-contentdoc.claim: Content loop detection hashes chunks of streamed text, detects identical chunks that appear frequently within a short distance, and is disabled inside code blocks.

g-contentthr.claim: A chunk is only considered once it has occurred at least the content threshold number of times, and the most recent occurrences are then tested for how close together they are.

g-events.claim: Each stream event is passed to `addAndCheck`; a count above 1 yields `LoopDetected` and stops, and a count of exactly 1 stops for recovery unless the remaining turn budget is 1 or less.

g-llmgate.claim: At the start of a turn, the model-based check runs only when the turns in the current prompt have reached `LLM_CHECK_AFTER_TURNS` and at least `llmCheckInterval` turns have passed since the last check.

g-llmconst.claim: The model-based check includes the 20 most recent turns and is activated after 30 turns in a single prompt.

g-interval.claim: The check interval defaults to 10 turns, with a minimum of 5 and a maximum of 15.

g-conf.claim: The confidence threshold for the model-based check is 0.9, and the double-check model alias is `loop-detection-double-check`.

g-history.claim: The model-based check takes the last `LLM_LOOP_CHECK_HISTORY_COUNT` entries of the client's history.

g-below.claim: If the first model's confidence is below the threshold, the check interval is updated and no loop is reported.

g-unavailable.claim: If the double-check model is not available, a loop is reported on the first model's result alone.

g-double.claim: Otherwise the same contents are sent to the double-check model.

g-confirm.claim: When the double-check model returns a result with confidence at or above the threshold, a loop is reported; when it returns a result below the threshold, the interval is updated; in every other case no loop is reported.

g-adapt.claim: The next check interval is the minimum plus the range multiplied by one minus the confidence, so higher confidence gives a shorter interval.

g-turnstart.claim: At the start of a turn, a detection count above 1 yields `LoopDetected` and returns; a count of exactly 1 goes to `_recoverFromLoop`, unless the turn budget is 1 or less.

g-recover.claim: Recovery clears the detection flag, builds a feedback message beginning `System: Potential loop detected`, and calls `sendMessageStream` again with that message and one fewer bounded turn.

g-disable.claim: The turn-start check returns a count of 0 when detection is disabled for the session or by configuration.

o-window.claim: The detector reads a window of recent events limited by `MAX_EVENTS_TO_SCAN_FOR_STUCK_DETECTION` and keeps only those after the last user message.

o-thr.claim: The default thresholds are 4 for action-observation, 3 for action-error, 3 for monologue and 6 for the alternating pattern.

o-scenarios.claim: `is_stuck` calls five checks in order: same action and observation, same action with errors, monologue, alternating action-observation, and a context window error check.

o-s1.claim: Scenario 1 reports stuck when the most recent threshold actions are all equal and the most recent threshold observations are all equal.

o-s2.claim: Scenario 2 reports stuck when the action-error streak is greater than the threshold.

o-nudge.claim: A nudge is returned when the action-error streak equals the threshold exactly and that error event has not been nudged before; its text names the tool and the error.

o-mono.claim: The monologue check counts consecutive agent messages, stopping at a user message or any action or observation, and reports stuck when the count reaches the threshold.

o-run.claim: `_check_stuck_or_nudge` first emits any nudge as a user-role message and returns False; otherwise, if `is_stuck()` is true, it sets the execution status to STUCK and returns True.

o-defaults.claim: The local conversation defaults to `max_iteration_per_run` of 500 and `stuck_detection` of True.

o-maxiter.claim: When the iteration count reaches `max_iteration_per_run` and the run has not finished, the status is set to ERROR with a maximum-iterations message.

l-default.claim: `DEFAULT_RECURSION_LIMIT` is read from the `LANGGRAPH_DEFAULT_RECURSION_LIMIT` environment variable and defaults to 10007.

l-stop.claim: The loop's stop step is set to the current step plus the configured `recursion_limit` plus 1.

l-tick.claim: On each tick, if the step is greater than the stop step, the status is set to `out_of_steps` and the tick returns False.

l-raise.claim: When the loop status is `out_of_steps`, a `GraphRecursionError` is raised with a message suggesting a higher `recursion_limit`.

l-more.claim: `_are_more_steps_needed` returns True when remaining steps are below 2 and the response has tool calls, or below 1 when all tool calls return directly.

l-sorry.claim: When more steps are needed, the agent returns a message with the content `Sorry, need more steps to process this request.`

l-deprecated.claim: The `AgentState` and `AgentStatePydantic` classes in the prebuilt module are marked deprecated.

x-doc.claim: The turn function's documentation says it runs a loop in which the model replies with function calls or an assistant message, and function call output is sent back in the next sampling request.

x-comment.claim: A comment says that as long as compaction brings the context well below the token limit, an infinite loop is not a concern.

x-exit.claim: The loop has a branch that is entered when no follow-up is needed.

g-cap.claim: The number of turns for a send is bounded to at most `MAX_TURNS`.

o-stub.claim: `_is_stuck_context_window_error` contains only a TODO comment and returns False.

o-streak.claim: The action-error streak counts the most recent pairs whose action equals the latest action and whose observation is an `AgentErrorEvent`; the errors are not compared with each other.

o-alt.claim: The alternating check reports stuck when each recent action equals the action two positions before it and each recent observation equals the observation two positions before it.

o-thrparam.claim: The local conversation accepts a `stuck_detection_thresholds` parameter.

l-defaultuse.claim: The default run config sets `recursion_limit` to `DEFAULT_RECURSION_LIMIT`.

l-end.claim: `should_continue` does not route to tools when the last message is not an AI message with tool calls: it returns a post-model hook, a structured-response step, or END.

x-followup.claim: Follow-up is needed when the model needs follow-up or there is pending input.

x-break.claim: The loop breaks when the stop outcome says it should stop.

x-continue.claim: After the no-follow-up block ends with a break, the loop continues to its next iteration.

g-clear.claim: `clearDetection` resets only the detected flag and keeps the detection count, so the next detection is count 2.

g-reset.claim: `reset` clears the tool-call history and sets the detection count back to 0.

g-trim.claim: The tool-call history is trimmed to the last 5 times the loop threshold entries.

implementation.title: A loop detector in 95 lines of Python
implementation.intro: One class, standard library only. It combines Gemini CLI's exact-match cycle detection and warn-then-stop response with OpenHands' result-aware and error-streak rules. Feed it each tool call once it has finished; it answers continue, warn or stop.

mirrors.what: A tool call is fingerprinted as the SHA-256 of its name and JSON arguments
History is trimmed to 5 times the threshold
Cycles of length 1 to 5 are checked against the most recent calls
Each detection increments a counter; the first warns and the second stops
The warning does not reset the counter or the history, so a repeat is detection 2
A new prompt clears the history and the counter
Four identical call-and-result pairs in a row means stuck
The error streak counts how often the latest call has just errored, without comparing the errors
At exactly 3 errors in a row the model gets a nudge naming the tool and the error
More than 3 errors in a row means stuck

simplifications: Python, not TypeScript or the original Python: the logic is rewritten, not copied.
No repeated-text detector and no model-based check; only Gemini CLI's tool-call cycle detector is reproduced.
It checks a call after it has finished, so that results can be compared. Gemini CLI checks when the model requests the call, before it runs, so there the repeated call is stopped before executing.
There is no turn budget. In Gemini CLI a first detection stops the turn instead of warning when the turn budget is already used up; here a first detection always warns.
Two calls are the same when their name and arguments match. OpenHands also compares the agent's accompanying thought and the type of each event.
OpenHands' monologue and alternating-pattern checks are left out, and its 20-event window after the last user message is replaced by `reset()` on a new prompt.
A step is one call with its result and whether it was an error, so the same-result rule compares whole steps; OpenHands compares separate lists of actions and observations.
The nudge fires whenever the streak is exactly 3; OpenHands also remembers which error event it already nudged for.
Stopping is returned as a verdict for the caller to act on; the originals emit an event or set a conversation status.
Fingerprints use Python's JSON formatting, so the hash values differ from Gemini CLI's even though the comparison behaves the same.
